section.heading: 1.1. Four Ways to Represent a Function
Functions
section.paragraph: Functions arise whenever one quantity depends on another. Consider the following four situations.

list.item: The area $$A$$ of a circle depends on the radius $$r$$ of the circle. The rule that connects $$r$$ and $$A$$ is given by the equation $$A = \pi r^{2}$$ . With each positive number $$r$$ there is associated one value of $$A$$ , and we say that $$A$$ is a function of $$r$$ .

The human population of the world $$P$$ depends on the time $$t$$ . Table 1 gives estimates of the world population $$P$$ at time $$t$$ , for certain years. For instance, $$P \approx 2,560,000,000 \text{when} t = 1950$$ For each value of the time $$t$$ there is a corresponding value of $$P$$ , and we say that $$P$$ is a function of $$t$$ . Table 1 World Population Year Population (millions) 1900 1650 1910 1750 1920 1860 1930 2070 1940 2300 1950 2560 1960 3040 1970 3710 1980 4450 1990 5280 2000 6080 2010 6870

The cost $$C$$ of mailing an envelope depends on its weight $$w$$ . Although there is no simple formula that connects $$w$$ and $$C$$ , the post office has a rule for determining $$C$$ when $$w$$ is known.

The vertical acceleration $$a$$ of the ground as measured by a seismograph during an earthquake is a function of the elapsed time $$t$$ . Figure 1 shows a graph generated by seismic activity during the Northridge earthquake that shook Los Angeles in 1994. For a given value of $$t$$ , the graph provides a corresponding value of $$a$$ . The horizontal axis labeled t represents time in seconds and is displayed from 0 to 30 in increments of 5 units. The vertical axis labeled a represents acceleration in centimeter per square second and is displayed from below negative 50 to 100 in increments of 50. The curve in the form of a wave is almost centered about the horizontal axis. It begins at the point (0, 0), runs along the horizontal axis until approximately (5, 0), then rises and falls very closely as it progressively increases, reaching its sharp lowest point at approximately (12, negative 75) and reaches its sharp highest point at approximately (17, 125). The height of the curve then progressively decreases by rising and falling very closely and ends at (30, 0). Calif. section.paragraph: Each of these examples describes a rule whereby, given a number ( $$r$$ in Example A), another number $$(A)$$ is assigned. In each case we say that the second number is a function of the first number. If $$f$$ represents the rule that connects $$A$$ to $$r$$ in Example A, then we express this in function notation as $$A = f(r)$$ .
A function $$f$$ is a rule that assigns to each element $$x$$ in a set $$D$$ exactly one element, called $$f(x)$$ , in a set $$E$$ .

We usually consider functions for which the sets $$D$$ and $$E$$ are sets of real numbers. The set $$D$$ is called the domain of the function. The number $$f(x)$$ is the value of $$\mathbf{f}$$ at $$\mathbf{x}$$ and is read “ $$f$$ of $$x$$ .” The range of $$f$$ is the set of all possible values of $$f(x)$$ as $$x$$ varies throughout the domain. A symbol that represents an arbitrary number in the domain of a function $$f$$ is called an independent variable. A symbol that represents a number in the range of $$f$$ is called a dependent variable. In Example A, for instance, $$r$$ is the independent variable and $$A$$ is the dependent variable.

It’s helpful to think of a function as a machine (see Figure 2). If $$x$$ is in the domain of the function $$f$$ , then when $$x$$ enters the machine, it’s accepted as an input and the machine produces an output $$f(x)$$ according to the rule of the function. So we can think of the domain as the set of all possible inputs and the range as the set of all possible outputs. The preprogrammed functions in a calculator are good examples of a function as a machine. For example, if you input a number and press the squaring key, the calculator displays the output, the square of the input.

image.alt: Details A diagram shows a rectangular machine labeled f with openings on the left and the right sides. The left side provides an entry x into it with a right arrow and is labeled Input. The right side provides an exit f(x), with another rightward arrow, and is labeled Output.

section.paragraph: Another way to picture a function is by an arrow diagram as in Figure 3. Each arrow connects an element of $$D$$ to an element of $$E$$ . The arrow indicates that $$f(x)$$ is associated with $$x$$ , $$f(a)$$ is associated with $$a$$ , and so on.

image.alt: Details An arrow diagram shows two sets labeled D and E which are represented by two irregularly shaped figures, displayed side-by-side. Set D is on the left side and set E is on the right. A right arrow labeled f runs from D to E. Set D has elements x and a, in the order from top to bottom. Set E has elements f(x) and f(a) in the order from top to bottom. Arrows run from elements of the left side to elements of the right side as follows: x to f(x); a to f(a). A point is marked on each of sets D and E, and a right arrow runs between them.

section.paragraph: Perhaps the most useful method for visualizing a function is its graph. If $$f$$ is a function with domain $$D$$ , then its graph is the set of ordered pairs
$$\left\{ \left( \left. x,f(x) \right) \middle| x \in D \right. \right\}$$

(Notice that these are input-output pairs.) In other words, the graph of $$f$$ consists of all points $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ in the coordinate plane such that $$y = f(x)$$ and $$x$$ is in the domain of $$f$$ .

The graph of a function $$f$$ gives us a useful picture of the behavior or “life history” of a function. Since the $$y$$ -coordinate of any point $$\left( {x,y} \right)$$ on the graph is $$y = f(x)$$ , we can read the value of $$f(x)$$ from the graph as being the height of the graph above the point $$x$$ . (See Figure 4.) The graph of $$f$$ also allows us to picture the domain of $$f$$ on the $$x$$ -axis and its range on the $$y$$ -axis as in Figure 5.

image.alt: Details A curve and three vertical line segments are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed with tick marks 0, 1, 2, and x, in the order from left to right. The curve enters the second quadrant above the x axis, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point on the y axis, then goes down and to the right in the first quadrant, becoming concave up, and reaches a low point directly above the tick mark 1 on the x axis. The curve then goes up and to the right, now again concave down to reach its highest point, and then goes down and to the right. Vertical line segments from the tick marks 1, 2, and x on the x axis extend upward and reach the curve. The heights of the vertical line segments from tick marks 1 and 2 are labeled f(1) and f(2), respectively. The height of the vertical line segment from tick mark x is labeled f(x). This vertical line segment intersects the curve at the labeled point (x, f(x)).

Details A curve is graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The curve, y = f(x), begins with a solid dot above the x axis, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches its high point, then goes down and to the right, and ends with a solid dot. From the beginning and ending points of the curve, dashed vertical line segments are dropped to the x axis, parallel to the y axis. The horizontal distance between these two dashed vertical line segments is labeled Domain. Also from the beginning and the high points of the curve, dashed horizontal line segments are drawn to the y axis, parallel to the x axis. The vertical distance between these two dashed horizontal line segments is labeled Range.

example.heading: Example 1
example.paragraph: The graph of a function $$f$$ is shown in Figure 6.

list.item: (a) Find the values of $$f(1)$$ and $$f(5)$$ .
(b) What are the domain and range of $$f$$ ?

image.alt: Details A curve is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed from negative 2 to 8 in increments of 1 unit. The y axis is displayed from negative 3 to 5 in increments of 1 unit. The curve begins at the point (0, 1), goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches a high point at (2, 4), goes down and to the right, becoming concave up at approximately (4, 1.2), crosses the x axis at approximately (4.6, 0), reaches a low point at approximately (6.2, negative 2), then goes up and to the right, and ends at the point (7, 0).

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) We see from Figure 6 that the point $$\left( {1,3} \right)$$ lies on the graph of $$f$$ , so the value of $$f$$ at $$1$$ is $$f(1) = 3$$ . (In other words, the point on the graph that lies above $$x = 1$$ is $$3$$ units above the $$x$$ -axis.) When $$x = 5$$ , the graph lies about $$0.7$$ units below the $$x$$ -axis, so we estimate that $$f(5) \approx - 0.7$$ .

(b) We see that $$f(x)$$ is defined when $$0 \leqslant x \leqslant 7$$ , so the domain of $$f$$ is the closed interval $$\left\lbrack {0,7} \right\rbrack$$ . Notice that $$f$$ takes on all values from $$- 2$$ to $$4$$ , so the range of $$f$$ is $$\left\{ y \middle| - 2 \leqslant y \leqslant 4 \right\} = \lbrack - 2,4\rbrack$$

example.paragraph: The notation for intervals is given in Appendix A.

section.paragraph: In calculus, the most common method of defining a function is by an algebraic equation. For example, the equation $$y = 2x - 1$$ defines $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$ . We can express this in function notation as $$f(x) = 2x - 1$$ .

example.heading: Example 2
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph and find the domain and range of each function.
Solution

list.item: (a) The equation of the graph is $$y = 2x - 1$$ , and we recognize this as being the equation of a line with slope $$2$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$- 1$$ . (Recall the slope-intercept form of the equation of a line: $$y = mx + b$$ . See Appendix B.) This enables us to sketch a portion of the graph of $$f$$ in Figure 7. The expression $$2x - 1$$ is defined for all real numbers, so the domain of $$f$$ is the set of all real numbers, which we denote by $$\mathbb{R}$$ . The graph shows that the range is also $$\mathbb{R}$$ . Figure 7 Details A line with positive slope is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The line labeled y = 2 x minus 1 enters the bottom left of the viewing window in the third quadrant, goes up and to the right, crosses the y axis at (0, negative 1), then crosses the x axis at (1/2, 0), and exits the top right of the viewing window in the first quadrant.

(b) Since $$g(2) = 2^{2} = 4$$ and $$g\left( {- 1} \right) = \left( {- 1} \right)^{2} = 1$$ , we could plot the points $$(2,4)$$ and $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ , together with a few other points on the graph, and join them to produce the graph (Figure 8). The equation of the graph is $$y = x^{2}$$ , which represents a parabola (see Appendix C). The domain of $$g$$ is $$\mathbb{R}$$ . The range of $$g$$ consists of all values of $$g(x)$$ , that is, all numbers of the form $$x^{2}$$ . But $$x^{2} \geqslant 0$$ for all numbers $$x$$ and any positive number $$y$$ is a square. So the range of $$g$$ is $$\left\{ y \middle| y \geqslant 0 \right\} = \lbrack 0,\infty)$$ . This can also be seen from Figure 8. example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = 2x^{2} - 5x + 1$$ and $$h \neq 0$$ , evaluate $$\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}$$ .
Solution We first evaluate $$f\left( {a + h} \right)$$ by replacing $$x$$ by $$a + h$$ in the expression for $$f(x)$$ :
Then we substitute into the given expression and simplify:

$$\begin{array}{l} {\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h} = \frac{\left( {2a^{2} + 4ah + 2h^{2} - 5a - 5h + 1} \right) - \left( {2a^{2} - 5a + 1} \right)}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}} = \frac{2a^{2} + 4ah + 2h^{2} - 5a - 5h + 1 - 2a^{2} + 5a - 1}{h}} \\ {\phantom{\frac{f\left( {a + h} \right) - f(a)}{h}} = {\frac{4ah + 2h^{2} - 5h}{h} = 4a + 2h - 5}} \end{array}$$
The expression
$$\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$$
in Example 3 is called a difference quotient and occurs frequently in calculus. As we will see in Chapter 2, it represents the average rate of change of $$f(x)$$ between $$x = a$$ and $$x = a + h$$ .

section.heading: Representations of Functions
section.paragraph: We consider four different ways to represent a function:

If a single function can be represented in all four ways, it’s often useful to go from one representation to another to gain additional insight into the function. (In Example 2, for instance, we started with algebraic formulas and then obtained graphs.) But certain functions are described more naturally by one method than by another. With this in mind, let’s reexamine the four situations that we considered at the beginning of this section.

list.item: The most useful representation of the area of a circle as a function of its radius is probably the algebraic formula $$A = \pi r^{2}$$ or, in function notation, $$A(r) = \pi r^{2}$$ . It is also possible to compile a table of values or sketch a graph (half a parabola). Because a circle has to have a positive radius, the domain is $$\left\{ r \middle| r > 0 \right\} = \left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ and the range is also $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ .

We are given a description of the function in words: $$P(t)$$ is the human population of the world at time $$t$$ . Let’s measure $$t$$ so that $$t = 0$$ corresponds to the year 1900. Table 2 provides a convenient representation of this function. If we plot the ordered pairs in the table, we get the graph (called a scatter plot) in Figure 9. It too is a useful representation; the graph allows us to absorb all the data at once. What about a formula? Of course, it’s impossible to devise an explicit formula that gives the exact human population $$P(t)$$ at any time $$t$$ . But it is possible to find an expression for a function that approximates $$P(t)$$ . In fact, using methods explained in Section 1.4, we obtain an approximation for the population $$P$$ : $$P(t) \approx f{(t)} = {({1.43653 \times 10^{9}})} \cdot (1.01395)^{t}$$ Figure 10 shows that it is a reasonably good “fit.” The function $$f$$ is called a mathematical model for population growth. In other words, it is a function with an explicit formula that approximates the behavior of our given function. We will see, however, that the ideas of calculus can be applied to a table of values; an explicit formula is not necessary. Table 2 World Population $$t$$ (years since 1900) Population (millions) 0 1650 10 1750 20 1860 30 2070 40 2300 50 2560 60 3040 70 3710 80 4450 90 5280 100 6080 110 6870 Figure 9 Details Twelve points are graphed on a coordinate plane. The horizontal axis t is labeled Years since 1900 and is displayed from 0 to 120 in increments of 20 years. The vertical axis P is displayed from 0 to 7 billion in increments of 1 billion. The points are plotted at (0, 1650 million), (10, 1750 million), (20, 1860 million), (30, 2070 million), (40, 2300 million), (50, 2560 million), (60, 3040 million), (70, 3710 million), (80, 4450 million), (90, 5280 million), (100, 6080 million), and (110, 6870 million). The vertical axis P is displayed from 0 to 7 billion in increments of 1 billion. The data points are plotted at (0, 1650 million), (10, 1750 million), (20, 1860 million), (30, 2070 million), (40, 2300 million), (50, 2560 million), (60, 3040 million), (70, 3710 million), (80, 4450 million), (90, 5280 million), (100, 6080 million), and (110, 6870 million). The curve begins at approximately (0, 1500 million), goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, concave up, and grazes the points which are plotted at x = 20, x = 70, and x = 80. The plotted points lie closely above the curve from x = 0 to x = 10, lie closely below the curve from x = 20 to x = 70, again lie above the curve from x = 80 to x = 110. The function $$P$$ is typical of the functions that arise whenever we attempt to apply calculus to the real world. We start with a verbal description of a function. Then we may be able to construct a table of values of the function, perhaps from instrument readings in a scientific experiment. Even though we don’t have complete knowledge of the values of the function, we will see throughout the book that it is still possible to perform the operations of calculus on such a function.

Again, the function is described in words: Let $$C(w)$$ be the cost of mailing a large envelope with weight $$w$$ . The rule that the US Postal Service used as of 2019 is as follows: The cost is $$1$$ dollar for up to $$1$$ oz, plus $$15$$ cents for each additional ounce (or less) up to $$13$$ oz. A table of values is the most convenient representation for this function (see Table 3), though it is possible to sketch a graph (see Example 10). Table 3 $$w$$ (ounces) $$C(w)$$ (dollars) $$0 < w \leqslant 1$$ 1.00 $$1 < w \leqslant 2$$ 1.15 $$2 < w \leqslant 3$$ 1.30 $$3 < w \leqslant 4$$ 1.45 $$4 < w \leqslant 5$$ 1.60 $$\vdots$$ $$\vdots$$ A function defined by a table of values is called a tabular function.

The graph shown in Figure 1 is the most natural representation of the vertical acceleration function $$a(t)$$ . It’s true that a table of values could be compiled, and it is even possible to devise an approximate formula. But everything a geologist needs to know—amplitudes and patterns—can be seen easily from the graph. (The same is true for the patterns seen in electrocardiograms of heart patients and polygraphs for lie-detection.)

section.paragraph: In the next example we sketch the graph of a function that is defined verbally.

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: When you turn on a hot-water faucet that is connected to a hot-water tank, the temperature $$T$$ of the water depends on how long the water has been running. Draw a rough graph of $$T$$ as a function of the time $$t$$ that has elapsed since the faucet was turned on.

Solution The initial temperature of the running water is close to room temperature because the water has been sitting in the pipes. When the water from the hot-water tank starts flowing from the faucet, $$T$$ increases quickly. In the next phase, $$T$$ is constant at the temperature of the heated water in the tank. When the tank is drained, $$T$$ decreases to the temperature of the water supply. This enables us to make the rough sketch of $$T$$ as a function of $$t$$ shown in Figure 11.

The curve begins on the positive vertical axis, goes almost linearly upward to the right, turns, running horizontally to the right, then goes down and to the right, again turns and runs almost horizontally rightward, parallel to the horizontal axis.

section.paragraph: In the following example we start with a verbal description of a function in a physical situation and obtain an explicit algebraic formula. The ability to do this is a useful skill in solving calculus problems that ask for the maximum or minimum values of quantities.

section.paragraph: In the next example we find the domain of a function that is defined algebraically. If a function is given by a formula and the domain is not stated explicitly, we use the following domain convention: the domain of the function is the set of all inputs for which the formula makes sense and gives a real-number output.

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: Find the domain of each function.
Solution

list.item: (a) Because the square root of a negative number is not defined (as a real number), the domain of $$f$$ consists of all values of $$x$$ such that $$x + 2 \geqslant 0$$ . This is equivalent to $$x \geqslant - 2$$ , so the domain is the interval $$\lbrack - 2,\infty)$$ .

(b) Since $$g(x) = \frac{1}{x^{2} - x} = \frac{1}{x\left( {x - 1} \right)}$$ and division by $$0$$ is not allowed, we see that $$g(x)$$ is not defined when $$x = 0$$ or $$x = 1$$ . So the domain of $$g$$ is $$\left\{ x \middle| x \neq 0,x \neq 1 \right\}$$ which could also be written in interval notation as $$\left( {- \infty,0} \right) \cup \left( {0,1} \right) \cup \left( {1,\infty} \right)$$

section.heading: Which Rules Define Functions?
section.paragraph: Not every equation defines a function. The equation $$y = x^{2}$$ defines $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$ because the equation determines exactly one value of $$y$$ for each value of $$x$$ . However, the equation $$y^{2} = x$$ does not define $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$ because some input values $$x$$ correspond to more than one output $$y$$ ; for instance, for the input $$x = 4$$ the equation gives the outputs $$y = 2$$ and $$y = - 2$$ .

Similarly, not every table defines a function. Table 3 defined $$C$$ as a function of $$w$$ —each package weight $$w$$ corresponds to exactly one mailing cost. On the other hand, Table 4 does not define $$y$$ as a function of $$x$$ because some input values $$x$$ in the table correspond to more than one output $$y$$ ; for instance, the input $$x = 5$$ gives the outputs $$y = 7$$ and $$y = 8$$ .
section.heading: Table 4
section.paragraph: What about curves drawn in the $$\mathit{xy}$$ -plane? Which curves are graphs of functions? The following test gives an answer.

note.title: The Vertical Line Test
note.heading: The Vertical Line Test
note.paragraph: A curve in the $$xy$$ -plane is the graph of a function of $$x$$ if and only if no vertical line intersects the curve more than once.

section.paragraph: The reason for the truth of the Vertical Line Test can be seen in Figure 13. If each vertical line $$x = a$$ intersects a curve only once, at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ , then exactly one function value is defined by $$f(a) = b$$ . But if a line $$x = a$$ intersects the curve twice, at $$\left( {a,b} \right)$$ and $$\left( {a,c} \right)$$ , then the curve can’t represent a function because a function can’t assign two different values to $$a$$ .

section.paragraph: For example, the parabola $$x = y^{2} - 2$$ shown in Figure 14(a) is not the graph of a function of $$x$$ because, as you can see, there are vertical lines that intersect the parabola twice. The parabola, however, does contain the graphs of two functions of $$x$$ . Notice that the equation $$x = y^{2} - 2$$ implies $$y^{2} = x + 2$$ , so $$y = \pm \sqrt{x + 2}$$ . Thus the upper and lower halves of the parabola are the graphs of the functions $$f(x) = \sqrt{x + 2}$$ [from Example 6(a)] and $$g(x) = - \sqrt{x + 2}$$ . [See Figures 14(b) and (c).]

section.paragraph: We observe that if we reverse the roles of $$x$$ and $$y$$ , then the equation $$x = h(y) = y^{2} - 2$$ does define $$x$$ as a function of $$y$$ (with $$y$$ as the independent variable and $$x$$ as the dependent variable). The graph of the function $$h$$ is the parabola in Figure 14(a).
section.heading: Piecewise Defined Functions
section.paragraph: The functions in the following four examples are defined by different formulas in different parts of their domains. Such functions are called piecewise defined functions.

example.heading: Example 7
example.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is defined by
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} {1 - x} & {{if}x \leqslant - 1} \\ x^{2} & {{if}x > - 1} \end{cases}$$
Evaluate $$f\left( {- 2} \right)$$ , $$f\left( {- 1} \right)$$ , and $$f(0)$$ and sketch the graph.

Solution Remember that a function is a rule. For this particular function the rule is the following: First look at the value of the input $$x$$ . If it happens that $$x \leqslant - 1$$ , then the value of $$f(x)$$ is $$1 - x$$ . On the other hand, if $$x > - 1$$ , then the value of $$f(x)$$ is $$x^{2}$$ . Note that even though two different formulas are used, $$f$$ is one function, not two.

$$\begin{array}{l} {{Since} - 2 \leqslant - 1,{we have}f( - 2) = 1 - ( - 2) = 3.} \\ {{Since} - 1 \leqslant - 1,{we have}f( - 1) = 1 - ( - 1) = 2.} \\ {{Since}0 > - 1,{we have}f(0) = 0^{2} = 0.} \end{array}$$

How do we draw the graph of $$f$$ ? We observe that if $$x \leqslant - 1$$ , then $$f(x) = 1 - x$$ , so the part of the graph of $$f$$ that lies to the left of the vertical line $$x = - 1$$ must coincide with the line $$y = 1 - x$$ , which has slope $$- 1$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$1$$ . If $$x > - 1$$ , then $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ , so the part of the graph of $$f$$ that lies to the right of the line $$x = - 1$$ must coincide with the graph of $$y = x^{2}$$ , which is a parabola. This enables us to sketch the graph in Figure 15. The solid dot indicates that the point $$\left( {- 1,2} \right)$$ is included on the graph; the open dot indicates that the point $$\left( {- 1,1} \right)$$ is excluded from the graph.

The y axis is displayed from below 0 to beyond 1 in increments of 1 unit. section.paragraph: The next example of a piecewise defined function is the absolute value function. Recall that the absolute value of a number $$a$$ , denoted by $$|a|$$ , is the distance from $$a$$ to $$0$$ on the real number line. Distances are always positive or $$0$$ , so we have
$$|a| \geqslant 0 { \text{for every number} a}$$
For a more extensive review of absolute values, see Appendix A.
For example,
$$\left| 3 \middle| = 3 \middle| - 3 \middle| = 3 \middle| 0 \middle| = 0 \middle| \sqrt{2} - 1 \middle| = \sqrt{2} - 1 \middle| 3 - \pi \middle| = \pi - 3 \right.$$
In general, we have
$$\begin{array}{ll} {|a| = a} & {{if}a \geqslant 0} \\ {|a| = - a} & {{if}a < 0} \end{array}$$
(Remember that if $$a$$ is negative, then $$- a$$ is positive.)

example.heading: Example 8
example.paragraph: Sketch the graph of the absolute value function $$f(x) = |x|$$ .
Solution From the preceding discussion we know that
$$|x| = \begin{cases} x & {{if}x \geqslant 0} \\ {- x} & {{if}x < 0} \end{cases}$$

Using the same method as in Example 7, we see that the graph of $$f$$ coincides with the line $$y = x$$ to the right of the $$y$$ -axis and coincides with the line $$y = - x$$ to the left of the $$y$$ -axis (see Figure 16).

image.alt: Details An absolute value function is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve, y = abs(x), which is symmetric about the y axis, has two parts. The first part enters the top left of the viewing window in the second quadrant, goes linearly down and to the right, and reaches the origin. From the origin, the second part goes linearly up and to the right in the first quadrant.

example.heading: Example 9
example.paragraph: Find a formula for the function $$f$$ graphed in Figure 17.

image.alt: Details A curve with three parts is graphed on the x y coordinate plane on the grid lines. The x axis is displayed from 0 to 5 in increments of 1 unit. The y axis is displayed from 0 to 2 in increments of 1 unit. The first part begins at (0, 0), goes linearly up to the right in the first quadrant until the point (1, 1). From the point (1, 1), the second part goes linearly down and to the right, and ends on the x axis at (2, 0). The third part begins at (2, 0), running horizontally to the right along the x axis.

example.paragraph: Solution The line through $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ and $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ has slope $$m = 1$$ and $$y$$ -intercept $$b = 0$$ , so its equation is $$y = x$$ . Thus, for the part of the graph of $$f$$ that joins $$\left( {0,0} \right)$$ to $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ , we have
$$f(x) = x {if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1$$
The line through $$\left( {1,1} \right)$$ and $$\left( {2,0} \right)$$ has slope $$m = - 1$$ , so its point-slope form is
$$y - 0 = \left( {- 1} \right)\left( {x - 2} \right)$$
or
So we have
$$f(x) = 2 - x {if}1 < x \leqslant 2$$
We also see that the graph of $$f$$ coincides with the $$x$$ -axis for $$x > 2$$ . Putting this information together, we have the following three-piece formula for $$f$$ :
$$f(x) = \begin{cases} x & {{if}0 \leqslant x \leqslant 1} \\ {2 - x} & {{if}1 < x \leqslant 2} \\ 0 & {{if}x > 2} \end{cases}$$
The point-slope form of the equation of a line is $$y - y_{1} = m\left( x - x_{1} \right)$$ . See Appendix B.

example.heading: Example 10
example.paragraph: In Example C at the beginning of this section we considered the cost $$C(w)$$ of mailing a large envelope with weight $$w$$ . In effect, this is a piecewise defined function because, from Table 3, we have

$$C(w) = \left\{ \begin{array}{cl} 1.00 & {{if}0 < w \leqslant 1} \\ 1.15 & {{if}1 < w \leqslant 2} \\ 1.30 & {{if}2 < w \leqslant 3} \\ 1.45 & {{if}3 < w \leqslant 4} \\ \vdots & \end{array} \right.$$
The graph is shown in Figure 18.

section.paragraph: Looking at Figure 18, you can see why a function like the one in Example 10 is called a step function.
section.heading: Even and Odd Functions
section.paragraph: If a function $$f$$ satisfies $$f\left( {- x} \right) = f(x)$$ for every number $$x$$ in its domain, then $$f$$ is called an even function. For instance, the function $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ is even because

The geometric significance of an even function is that its graph is symmetric with respect to the $$y$$ -axis (see Figure 19). This means that if we have plotted the graph of $$f$$ for $$x \geqslant 0$$ , we obtain the entire graph simply by reflecting this portion about the $$y$$ -axis.

image.alt: Details A curve, two vertical line segments, and a horizontal line segment are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve is symmetric about the y axis. It enters the second quadrant at the top left of the viewing window, goes down and to the right, concave down, crosses the negative x axis, becomes concave up, reaches its low point on the negative y axis, then goes up and to the right by crossing the positive x axis, becoming concave down, and exits the top right of the viewing window in the first quadrant. Two points are plotted on the curve: one in the second quadrant, the other in the first quadrant, directly across each other. From the plotted points, vertical line segments are drawn to the x axis: the one meeting the negative x axis at the point labeled negative x has height f(negative x), the other meeting the positive x axis at the point labeled x has height f(x). Both the vertical distances are equal in length. A horizontal line segment connects the two plotted points. The horizontal distance from the y axis to each of the plotted points is equal.

section.paragraph: If $$f$$ satisfies $$f\left( {- x} \right) = - f(x)$$ for every number $$x$$ in its domain, then $$f$$ is called an odd function. For example, the function $$f(x) = x^{3}$$ is odd because
$$f\left( {- x} \right) = \left( {- x} \right)^{3} = - x^{3} = - f(x)$$

The graph of an odd function is symmetric about the origin (see Figure 20). If we already have the graph of $$f$$ for $$x \geqslant 0$$ , we can obtain the entire graph by rotating this portion through $$180^{{^\circ}}$$ about the origin.

image.alt: Details A curve, two vertical line segments, and two diagonal line segments are graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The curve enters the third quadrant, goes down and to the right through a marked point directly below a tick mark negative x, concave up, reaches a low point, goes upward to the right through the origin, then enters into the first quadrant, concave down, reaches a high point, and then goes down to the right through another marked point which is directly above a tick mark x. A vertical line segment extends downward in the third quadrant from the tick mark negative x on the x axis to the marked point on the curve. Another vertical line segment extends upward in the first quadrant from the tick mark x on the positive x axis to the marked point on the curve. This vertical distance is labeled f(x). Both the vertical line segments are equal in length. A diagonal line segment is drawn from the origin to each of the two marked points. The direct distance from the origin to each of the plotted points is the same.

example.heading: Example 11
example.paragraph: Determine whether each of the following functions is even, odd, or neither even nor odd.
Solution

list.item: (a) $$\begin{array}{l} {{f( - x)} = {{( - x)}^{5} + ( - x) = {( - 1)}^{5}x^{5} + ( - x)}} \\ {\phantom{f( - x)} = {- x^{5} - x = - (x^{5} + x)}} \\ {\phantom{f( - x)} = {- f(x)}} \end{array}$$ Therefore $$f$$ is an odd function.
(b) $$g\left( {- x} \right) = 1 - \left( {- x} \right)^{4} = 1 - x^{4} = g(x)$$ So $$g$$ is even.

(c) $$h\left( {- x} \right) = 2\left( {- x} \right) - \left( {- x} \right)^{2} = - 2x - x^{2}$$ Since $$h\left( {- x} \right) \neq h(x)$$ and $$h\left( {- x} \right) \neq - h(x)$$ , we conclude that $$h$$ is neither even nor odd.

section.heading: Increasing and Decreasing Functions
section.paragraph: The graph shown in Figure 22 rises from $$A$$ to $$B$$ , falls from $$B$$ to $$C$$ , and rises again from $$C$$ to $$D$$ . The function $$f$$ is said to be increasing on the interval $$\left\lbrack {a,b} \right\rbrack$$ , decreasing on $$\left\lbrack {b,c} \right\rbrack$$ , and increasing again on $$\left\lbrack {c,d} \right\rbrack$$ . Notice that if $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ are any two numbers between $$a$$ and $$b$$ with $$x_{1} < x_{2}$$ , then $$f\left( x_{1} \right) < f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ . We use this as the defining property of an increasing function.

image.alt: Details Four points, a curve, and six vertical line segments are graphed in the first quadrant of the x y coordinate plane. The x axis is displayed with tick marks a, x_1, x_2, b, c, and d, at irregular intervals, in the order from left to right. The curve y = f(x) begins at x = a in the first quadrant with a labeled point A, goes up and to the right, concave down, reaches a high point labeled B at x = b, then goes down and to the right, becoming concave up, reaches a low point labeled C at x = c, goes up and to the right, and ends at x = d with the labeled point D. Vertical line segments are drawn from each of the tick marks on the x axis to the curve. The height of the vertical line segment at x = x_1 is labeled f(x_1). The height of the vertical line segment at x = x_2 is labeled f(x_2).

section.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is called increasing on an interval $$I$$ if
$$f\left( x_{1} \right) < f\left( x_{2} \right) {whenever}x_{1} < x_{2}{in}I$$
It is called decreasing on $$I$$ if
$$f\left( x_{1} \right) > f\left( x_{2} \right) {whenever}x_{1} < x_{2}{in}I$$

In the definition of an increasing function it is important to realize that the inequality $$f\left( x_{1} \right) < f\left( x_{2} \right)$$ must be satisfied for every pair of numbers $$x_{1}$$ and $$x_{2}$$ in $$I$$ with $$x_{1} < x_{2}$$ .
You can see from Figure 23 that the function $$f(x) = x^{2}$$ is decreasing on the interval $$( - \infty,0\rbrack$$ and increasing on the interval $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ .

image.alt: Details An upward opening parabola, which is symmetric about the y axis, is graphed on the x y coordinate plane. The parabola labeled y = x^2, enters the top left of the viewing window in the second quadrant, goes down and to the right, reaches its vertex at the origin, and then goes up and to the right in the first quadrant, mirroring its earlier path.
